newsitem.title: GERMANY: Serb and Croat democracy vital for Bosnia - Bildt.
newsitem.headline: Serb and Croat democracy vital for Bosnia - Bildt.

text.p: Mass anti-government protests in Belgrade have alarmed the international community and could mean problems lie ahead for the Bosnian peace process, international peace coordinator Carl Bildt said on Wednesday.

Bosnia cannot be seen in isolation and the international community's goal is to see democracy gain ground throughout former Yugoslavia, Bildt said at a meeting of the executive committee of the multinational contact group on Bosnia.
"We are extremely concerned by what we now see from the authorities in Belgrade, who are trying to take democratic possibilities and rights away from people," he said.

"There have been threats to independent media and there has been the threat to the electoral process in Serbia...We attach very great importance to the democratic development in (Croatia and Serbia)."

In Serbia's biggest protests for five years, up to 150,000 people marched in Belgrade on Monday after authorities annulled opposition election victories. More marches were planned against a restaging of the elections on Wednesday.
In Zagreb more than 100,000 people gathered in the capital's main square this month to voice support for an independent radio station which the authorities tried to shut down.

"Our prime focus is Bosnia but we have said all the time that you can never see Bosnia in isolation, you have to look at developments throughout the region in terms of possibilities for refugees to return, for the independent media to operate and for the development of democracy," Bildt said.
"Our aim is to see democracy gradually gaining ground in Serbia, throughout Bosnia and in Croatia."
Bildt said he was appalled official Serbian television had aired no reports of the demonstrations. "That of course points to a very significant problem, to put it very mildly."
He said Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring had discussed the protests at a meeting with Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic in Brussels on Monday.
"We were not satisfied by the explanation given by Mr Milutinovic," Bildt said, and added that the committee in Bonn had talked about ways of moving the process forward.

The committee, formally known as the Steering Board, is holding two days of talks near Bonn to prepare for a meeting in London next week of the Peace Implementation Council (PIC), which is overseeing the year-old Bosnian peace settlement.
Bildt said the peace process agreed in Dayton, Ohio just over one year ago was on track. "Progress might be slow, but there is progress. And it is going in the direction that we aimed at in Dayton."

The Steering Board said on Tuesday it was seriously worried by the failure of Bosnia's ethnic groups to agree on the makeup of a council of ministers, or cabinet. It urged the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to establish a council of ministers without delay, Germany's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Bildt said: "The setting up of common structures that are truly and genuinely accepted by all three ethnic communities is really the long-term key to the peace procces.

"If that succeeds, then I think Bosnia will develop as a united country. If that fails, then it is easy to see that it will be difficult to contain the forces that are working to actually cement the partition that is there on the ground."
